Intel resmikan GPU D270: chip AI inference dengan memori sampai 480GB

Intel finally gave its inference chip a real name and a memory number big enough to make hyperscalers look twice: the GPU D270 can carry up to 480GB, triple what Nvidia's most common inference cards typically ship. Intel used the OCP Global Summit on October 12 to drop the codename and introduce the real product: the GPU D270, the first entry in a new Intel GPU D-Series built specifically for AI inference. For more than a year the chip was known only as Crescent Island, a placeholder that outlived its usefulness the moment Intel decided to actually ship the thing. Now it has specs, and the specs tell you exactly what Intel is betting on. The headline number is memory. Intel's reference design ships with 160GB of LPDDR5X, but the architecture lets outside manufacturers build cards carrying up to 480GB. That's not a typo or a rounding error, it's the whole strategy. Where Nvidia and AMD chase raw FLOPS with GDDR7 or HBM, Intel went the other way: cheaper, more abundant LPDDR5X, stacked high. The tradeoff shows up in bandwidth, 1.5TB per second, which trails the HBM-equipped cards from Nvidia and AMD but comes at a fraction of the cost and none of the current HBM supply crunch. On compute, the D270 delivers 1.3 peak petaflops of FP8 throughput across 32 Xe3 cores and 256 XMX engines, inside a 350-watt envelope. AMD's Instinct MI350P, by comparison, hits 2.3 petaflops of FP8, nearly double, but it draws up to 600 watts to get there. Intel isn't trying to out-muscle that chip. It's betting that a data center running thousands of inference requests a day cares more about tokens per watt and tokens per dollar than a FLOPS leaderboard. That bet lines up with where AI spending is actually headed. Training still grabs headlines, but inference, the actual running of models once they're built, now accounts for roughly two-thirds of AI compute demand, a shift that's reshaped what chipmakers are racing to build. Training runs reward raw FLOPS. Inference runs reward memory capacity, because the bottleneck is usually how much of a model and its context you can hold in memory at once, not how fast you can multiply matrices. Intel designed the D270 to be cheap and plentiful where Nvidia's H200 and Blackwell cards are expensive and supply constrained. Intel unveiled its Crescent Island GPU at Computex 2026, offering up to 480GB of LPDDR5X memory on the Xe3P architecture in a direct challenge to Nvidia's AI accelerator dominance. The chip targets inference workloads with a 350W air-cooled design, sidestepping the HBM shortage, but the software ecosystem question remains the critical variable for... - Intel's Crescent Island GPU competes with Nvidia accelerators - data center GPU for AI inference workloads

That supply problem is the real opening here. Nvidia has spent much of 2026 unable to make enough HBM-equipped GPUs to satisfy demand, and that scarcity has pushed every major cloud provider to look for alternatives. Google already runs its seventh-generation TPU, Ironwood, at scale. Microsoft has Maia 200 in production workloads and Maia 300 coming in 2027. Amazon has Trainium 3. Meta has its own MTIA chips. Those projects are custom silicon tied to each company's own cloud or data-center stack rather than merchant accelerators sold as standalone cards. Intel's D270 is different: it's merchant silicon, meaning any hyperscaler, cloud provider, or enterprise buyer can simply purchase it, the way they'd buy an Nvidia or AMD card. That's a narrower lane than building your own chip, but it's also the only lane open to a company that isn't Google, Microsoft, Amazon, or Meta. Frankly, Intel needs this win badly. The company has burned through multiple data-center GPU attempts, from Ponte Vecchio to Gaudi, without ever landing a product that cloud providers bought in volume. The D270 is Intel's clearest shot yet at becoming a credible third option in a market Nvidia still dominates with well over 80% share, according to most industry estimates, with AMD a distant second. Timing is the catch. Intel says the D270 is now sampling with customers, but there's no confirmed ship date for broad availability, and most signals point to a 2027 rollout rather than anything landing on racks this year. That's a long runway in a market moving as fast as AI infrastructure. By the time the D270 actually ships in volume, Nvidia will likely be deep into its next architecture cycle, and AMD's own roadmap won't stand still either. Still, naming the chip and publishing real numbers is a meaningful step past the vague teasers Intel offered through most of 2026. A 480GB memory ceiling and a 350-watt power budget give cloud buyers something concrete to model against their own inference costs, which is exactly the kind of decision Intel needs them making before the chip even ships.
